newsitem.title: USA: Uganda hopes to get approval under debt plan this week.
newsitem.headline: Uganda hopes to get approval under debt plan this week.

text.p: Disappointed at delays in implementing a debt relief plan for the very poorest counties, Uganda is hopeful it will get the green light this week from the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, diplomatic sources said on Sunday.

The African country has been singled out to be the first recipient of the long-awaited plan although actual assistance will be be probably not be made until April 1998, at the earliest, the sources said.

As Ugandan Prime Minister Kintu Musoke told a group of business executives attending a conference sponsored by the Corporate Council on Africa, the country has worked hard to bring about the reform that has made it a standout from slower moving states in the region.
"We hope that the agreement will finally come, although we had hoped that the funding would come sooner," a source said.

Unveiled with high hopes last year, the so-called Debt Initiative for Heavily Indebted Poor Countries has had anything but a smooth time, with quarrels developing among the rich industrial countries on how quickly the plan should move.

Initially Uganda, considered a test case for the programme, had hoped to get the funding by last September and even now there is some pressure to delay until 1999 to make certain the country does not stray from the reform path.
But the sources said the country has pushed reform for years and would continue doing so even without a new debt assistance plan. "We know this is the way we must go," the sources said.

The meeting of the business group in suburban Washington comes just before the semi-annual gathering of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank at which the new debt relief initiative for very poor countries will be a major topic of discussion.

Uganda, if no new problems emerge, will be the first country to benefit from the plan although it is expected to be closely followed by the Ivory Coast, Burkina Faso, and Bolivia. Some 33 or the 44 countries that could be eligible are in Africa.

The initiative, which combines the efforts of the IMF, World Bank and the Paris Club of creditor nations, is designed to provide poor countries that persevere with tough economic reforms with debt relief. Uganda has $3.4 billion in debt and hopes to receive $385 million.

While such assistance is critical to help very poor countries overwhelmed with debt including past loans from the lending agencies themselves, the meeting of African leaders and the business community underscored the spread of investment interest by the private sector in developing countries around the world.
During the Sunday gathering, the conference also heard a stong pitch for foreign investment from representatives from two other debt initiative candidates -- Ivory Coast and Mozambique.
The meeting of African officials, the first conference of this kind by the corporate council -- formed in 1992 to help generate activity by the private sector in Africa -- ends on Tuesday.
